sources.label: Positive lower density of large prime gaps · Introduction and main theorem

guides.title: Large prime gaps: from occurrence to positive frequency
guides.summary: The paper studies how often large gaps occur between consecutive primes. For each fixed threshold C, gaps exceeding C times the average scale form a positive proportion of every sufficiently long prefix of prime indices. That proportion may depend on C.
guides.question: Arbitrarily large prime gaps are known to occur. Can their frequency among prime indices also be controlled?
guides.paperClaim: Let $p_n$ be the nth prime. The main theorem states that, for each fixed $C>0$, there is $c(C)>0$ such that every sufficiently large N satisfies $\#\{n\le N:p_{n+1}-p_n>C\log p_n\}\ge c(C)N$. It also implies that the indices where $p_n/n$ strictly increases have positive lower asymptotic density.
guides.whyItMatters: Arbitrarily large gaps and a positive proportion of gaps above a fixed threshold are different conclusions. The count here gives equal weight to prime indices. A proportion of empty intervals indexed by integer starting points cannot directly replace it.
proofRoute: Construct nonnegative weights on two adjacent short intervals. The first interval detects a prime, while the weighted prime count in the second is suppressed.
Apply two second-moment estimates to turn the weighted information into a positive proportion of ordinary integer starting points.
Bound the number of starting points associated with each prime gap to count distinct consecutive gaps. Then use the prime number theorem to obtain the ratio corollary.
guides.scopeLabel: Scope prose and configured statement differ
guides.scopeNotes: The scope document describes only the positive-density corollary for increases of p_n/n. However, the Comparator selected by PrimeGaps.json and the theorem large_gaps_and_ratio_density in RatioCorollary.lean state both the large-gap count and the ratio corollary. The configured statement is broader than the scope prose.
guides.boundary: This documentation discrepancy remains unresolved. Proofweave has not run Comparator or checked all imported dependency proofs, so these notes do not certify either description.

terms.explanation: The limit inferior of the proportion in the first N positive integers. Positive lower density gives one positive lower bound for all sufficiently long prefixes.
Near a prime p, the average gap scale is described by $\log p$. After C is fixed, the density constant may depend on C.

The dyadic case of the Erdős similarity conjecture · Introduction and main theorem

guides.title: Erdős similarity: fixed geometric ratios and the dyadic case
guides.summary: This family contains two papers with different scopes. The earlier paper treats the dyadic sequence; the newer paper treats each fixed geometric ratio. They construct compact sets of measure close to one that avoid every nontrivial affine copy of the selected sequence.
guides.question: Can a set occupying almost all of the unit interval avoid every translation and nonzero dilation of a given infinite sequence?
guides.paperClaim: For each fixed $q\in(0,1)$ and $\eta\in(0,1)$, the October 2026 manuscript constructs $E_{q,\eta}\subset[0,1]$ of measure greater than $1-\eta$. For every real x and nonzero real s, some $n\ge1$ satisfies $x+s q^n\notin E_{q,\eta}$. The set may depend on q; a single set need not avoid all ratios at once.
guides.whyItMatters: The conclusion includes both positive and negative dilations. Geometric sequences are a particular class of infinite patterns. The result does not automatically extend to arbitrary infinite sets.
proofRoute: Construct a sparse open periodic blocking set that meets every translated, scale-normalized copy of the geometric sequence.
Organize randomized cell tests with a finite routing tree and separated windows of sequence indices. This controls the number of tests required by the continuous scale parameter.
Repair exceptional centers with small open neighborhoods. Use summable dilations and reflections to cover every nonzero scale, then take the complement to obtain a compact set.
guides.scopeLabel: The linked Lean scope covers only the dyadic case
guides.scopeNotes: The scope document, DyadicAvoidance Comparator, and configured solution entry use $q=1/2$, or the sequence $2^{-n}$. They include all translations and nonzero dilations of either sign.
guides.boundary: The dyadic coverage note does not transfer to the newer general-ratio paper in this family. Coverage for arbitrary fixed q needs a separate check. Proofweave has not replayed the full dependencies of the dyadic case.

terms.explanation: The entire set of points $x+sA$ for one translation x and one nonzero dilation s. All points of the sequence must be considered together.
For every chosen positive tolerance, the total length removed from the unit interval can be made smaller than that tolerance.

guides.title: Matrix multiplication: the 9/4 exponent, rectangular bounds, and arbitrary fields
guides.summary: Three manuscripts treat the 9/4 square-matrix exponent over the complex numbers, earlier square and rectangular bounds, and a separate bound over each fixed field. These notes keep their computation models, fields, and matrix shapes distinct.
guides.question: What asymptotic exponent can be achieved for the number of field operations needed to multiply matrices?
guides.paperClaim: The October manuscript claims $\omega\le9/4$ over the complex numbers: for each $\varepsilon>0$, the arithmetic cost is $O_\varepsilon(n^{9/4+\varepsilon})$. The earlier manuscript also gives $\alpha>0.465$ and $\omega(1,0.709,1)<2.092$. A separate paper gives $\omega(F)<2.371054886006746$ for each fixed field F.
guides.whyItMatters: These statements count field operations such as addition, subtraction, and multiplication. They concern asymptotic exponents. They do not give bit complexity, measured implementation speed, or a practical crossover size. The 9/4 conclusion cannot be applied directly to every field.
proofRoute: The 9/4 manuscript uses tensor block separation to turn structures independent in two variable groups into a full direct sum, while accounting for auxiliary construction costs.

Study discrete growth through polynomial multiplication and spectral methods. Compare upper and lower estimates to constrain the matrix multiplication exponent. The earlier manuscript also analyzes rectangular shapes.
The arbitrary-field manuscript uses staggered tensor extraction and recovery, combines capacity across recursion levels, and obtains the numerical bound from parameter certificates.
guides.scopeLabel: Main statement entries located for distinct fields and shapes
guides.scopeNotes: MatrixMultiplication selects three statements over the complex numbers. MatrixFields selects the arbitrary-field bound. Their Comparator statements explicitly define finite division-free arithmetic programs, operation costs, and an asymptotic model allowing any positive exponent slack.
guides.boundary: This batch checks main statements, configuration, and selected solution entries only. It does not replay tensor constructions, numerical certificates, or all dependencies, and does not turn asymptotic bounds into practical performance claims.

terms.explanation: The infimum of exponents describing the asymptotic arithmetic cost of square matrix multiplication. Exponent statements allow any positive epsilon slack.
The supremum of shape parameters a for which multiplying an $n\times n^a$ matrix by an $n^a\times n$ matrix still has exponent 2.

sources.label: Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions · Introduction and main theorem

guides.title: How a divergent reciprocal sum forces arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions
guides.summary: The paper bounds the size of subsets of a finite interval that contain no k-term arithmetic progression. It then deduces that a set of positive integers with a divergent reciprocal sum contains nontrivial arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The linked Lean scope selects this qualitative consequence.
guides.question: Must a set of positive integers contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions if its reciprocal sum diverges, even when its density is zero?
guides.paperClaim: For each fixed $k\ge3$, the paper gives $r_k(N)\le C_k N\exp(-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k})$, with positive constants that may depend on k. It deduces that every set A of positive integers with $\sum_{a\in A}1/a=\infty$ contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length with positive common difference.
guides.whyItMatters: A divergent reciprocal sum allows sets of density zero. A qualitative density-decay statement alone is therefore insufficient. The key bridge in the introduction sums the finite-interval estimate over dyadic intervals to obtain a summable bound that contradicts divergence.
proofRoute: Use density increments on structured regions to turn the absence of long arithmetic progressions into successive increases in local density.
Control losses in dimension and precision across weight levels so that the total interval-length loss over repeated increments has the required scale.

After obtaining the quantitative finite-interval bound, sum over dyadic intervals to deduce the reciprocal-sum conclusion. The implication runs from the quantitative bound to the qualitative corollary.
guides.scopeLabel: Lean selects the reciprocal-sum corollary, excluding the quantitative bound
guides.scopeNotes: The ErdosReciprocal Comparator states that, when the reciprocal terms are not summable, the set contains an arithmetic progression of any natural-number length k with common difference d>0. The configuration selects Progressions.Main as the solution entry. The scope document explicitly excludes the quantitative bound for $r_k(N)$.
guides.boundary: Checking or replaying this qualitative statement does not establish that the quantitative bound has also been verified in Lean. This batch does not audit the large dependency library imported by the solution entry.

terms.explanation: The largest cardinality of a subset of the integers from 1 to N containing no k-term arithmetic progression with nonzero common difference.
The qualitative conclusion asserts that a progression exists. A quantitative bound also controls the interval size and density that force one to occur.

sources.label: A linear cycle-and-edge decomposition of every graph · Introduction and main theorem

guides.title: Erdős–Gallai: partitioning all edges into linearly many cycles and single edges
guides.summary: The paper gives a positive constant C, independent of the graph, such that every finite simple undirected graph on n vertices has its edges partitioned into at most Cn simple cycles or single edges. Parts may share vertices, but cannot share edges.
guides.question: Regardless of graph density, can each edge be assigned exactly once using only linearly many cycles and single edges?
guides.paperClaim: There is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that the edge set of every finite simple undirected graph on n vertices can be partitioned into at most $Cn$ parts. Each part is the edge set of a simple cycle or a single edge. An edgeless graph may use the empty partition.
guides.whyItMatters: Forests contain no cycles, so single edges must be allowed. A cover can reuse edges, whereas this partition assigns each edge exactly once. A tree requires n−1 single edges, which also shows that a sublinear bound is impossible in general.
proofRoute: Split the graph by scale and extract subgraphs with cut expansion, reserving edges for later path connections.
Pair and identify selected vertices in chosen layers to form a smaller quotient graph, while controlling the edge-assignment cost outside the recursion.
Recurse on the quotient graph and lift cycles back using reserved edge-disjoint paths. Vertex savings and a strengthened induction bound pay the costs at each scale.
guides.scopeLabel: Main quantifiers and edge-partition requirements located
guides.scopeNotes: CycleDecomposition.MainStatement requires one common C for every n and every simple graph on Fin n. Parts must be pairwise edge-disjoint and their union must equal the original edge set. The definition permits simple cycles or single edges. The configuration selects erdos_gallai in CycleDecomposition.Main.
guides.boundary: This scope does not determine the optimal C or automatically cover other, stronger corollaries in the paper. This batch checks the main statement and entry only. It does not audit the full induction, path connections, or dependency proofs.

terms.explanation: Every edge occurs exactly once. Different parts may contain the same vertices.
The same C works for every graph and size. The quantifiers first assert the existence of C, then require the conclusion for all graphs.

sources.label: A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound · Introduction and main theorem

guides.title: Heilbronn triangles: an unbounded sequence of sizes versus all large sizes
guides.summary: The paper constructs point sets in the unit square with a uniform lower bound on the area of every triangle from three distinct points. The manuscript covers every sufficiently large cardinality. The selected Lean statement instead first gives constructions along a sequence of cardinalities tending to infinity.
guides.question: For n points in the unit square, how large can the smallest triangle determined by those points be?
guides.paperClaim: The paper claims fixed $\eta,c_1>0$ such that every sufficiently large n admits an n-point set whose triangle areas are all at least $c_1 n^{-2+\eta}$. This refutes the proposed eventual upper bound $O(n^{-2+\varepsilon})$ for every positive epsilon.
guides.whyItMatters: The bound must hold for every triple of distinct points, including exclusion of collinear triples. An unbounded sequence of sizes and every sufficiently large size are different scopes. The former already suffices to refute an upper bound asserted for all sufficiently large sizes.
proofRoute: Represent points as projections of integer column vectors, and express triangle area through the determinant of three columns.
Use two independent systems of congruence conditions to control small nonzero determinants and zero determinants separately. The latter handles collinearity.

Sample randomly and delete exceptional points to obtain a uniform area bound on the retained set. The manuscript uses further parameter and interpolation steps to reach every sufficiently large cardinality.
guides.scopeLabel: Lean covers an unbounded sequence; the manuscript claims more
guides.scopeNotes: The HeilbronnTriangle main statement constructs cardinalities n(j) tending to infinity and corresponding point sets. It gives a fixed positive exponent improvement for every triple of distinct points. Another statement uses this to refute the proposed eventual upper bound. The configuration selects HeilbronnTriangle.Main.
guides.boundary: The sequence statement does not justify reporting formalization for every sufficiently large n. Extending coverage requires locating a formal solution entry for the size-interpolation step. Full proofs and parameter dependencies still need replay.

terms.explanation: The minimum area over all triples of distinct points in the set. If three points are collinear, this minimum is zero.
The cardinality n(j) tends to infinity with j. The statement does not require every sufficiently large integer to equal some n(j).

nextChecks: Check the sequence construction and the refutation of the eventual upper bound as two separate statements.
Track the extension from selected sizes to all sufficiently large sizes as a separate coverage check.
